# Song, Hein 2005: an upper bound on `R¹` from a sequence of trees

Source: Y. S. Song, J. Hein, *Constructing minimal ancestral recombination graphs*, J. Comput. Biol. 12 (2005), 147--169, as stated in Gusfield et al. 2007, line 654 (the line numbers of Gusfield et al. are explained in `src/Gusfield2007/README.md`): "For any n by m matrix M, if P = T_1, T_2, ..., T_m is a sequence of time-ordered leaf-labeled trees in which T_i is compatible with site i in M,
for all i = 1, ..., m, then R¹(M) <= L(P)."

**Read:** the authors' copy, on Yun Song's page at Berkeley (28 pages, the text of the paper, not the journal's typesetting). It defers its definitions to Y. S. Song, J. Hein, *Parsimonious reconstruction of sequence evolution and haplotype blocks*, WABI 2003, and Gusfield et al. defer theirs to Y. S. Song, *Properties of subtree-prune-and-regraft operations on totally-ordered phylogenetic trees*, Ann. Comb. 10 (2006), 129--146. Both are on the same page, and both were read: the text layer of the first is unusable, so its pages were read as images.

What the source says, against `R_le_sprLength`:

- **Binary trees: the source's trees are binary.** "We consider leaf-labelled rooted binary trees"; an *ordered tree* is such a tree whose degree-3 vertices are totally ordered by age, no two equal (2005, Section 3.1; 2003, Section 2.1). `TimeOrderedTree` has real times, which can tie, and any number of children, as line 646 of Gusfield et al. does. So `R_le_sprLength` is stronger than the source here, and no hypothesis is added. Theorem 11 uses it on binary trees.
- **The SPR operation: the same, for the source's trees, with times in place of an order.** "Let `v` (resp. `v'`) denote the vertex in `T \ t` (resp. `T' \ t`) which is adjacent to the root of `t`. Suppose `v_i` and `v_j` are two internal vertices other than `v` and `v'`. If `v_i < v_j` before an SPR operation, then `v_i < v_j` after the SPR operation, and vice versa" (2003, Section 2.2; the same in 2006, Section 2.3). This comes on top of three kinds of operation on plain rooted trees, two of which move the root. `TimeOrderedTree.IsOrderedSPR` covers the three: the pruned subtree and what remains keep their nodes, the node above the subtree changes, and `prunedTime` is what moves the root. It keeps the *times* of those nodes, where the source keeps their *order*, so that a distance of the source is got on times chosen along the path: give the first tree any times, and each new vertex a time in its gap. Each step of the source is then a step of `IsOrderedSPR`, so the source's `L(P)` bounds `sprLength` of these times, and `R_le_sprLength` gives the source's inequality. This remark isn't in Lean. Nothing in `IsOrderedSPR` restricts the trees to be binary.
- **Compatibility: the same, but for constant columns.** "A tree `T` is said to be compatible with the informative column `c_i` if there exists an edge in `T` such that cutting the edge decomposes `T` into two connected components", one for each state, and "if the column `c_i` is not informative, then every `n`-leaved tree is considered compatible" (2005, Section 3.1). A column with one row in one state is compatible with every tree in Lean too, by the pendant edge. A constant column isn't: `TimeOrderedTree.CompatibleWith` follows line 646 of Gusfield et al., and the theorem says nothing for such a column. Gusfield et al. have no constant column, by their standing assumption.
- **What's claimed.** The source claims more than Gusfield et al. use: `d_SPR = d_rec` on ordered trees, and `min L(P) = R_min(S)`, equations (3), (5). This is all proved, with the columns not constant: see below.
- **The proof.** Neither paper proves any of this. Their argument is in words: "A subtree that gets pruned and regrafted in an SPR operation corresponds to the descendant subtree of a recombination vertex in an ARG" (2005, Section 3.3), "possible sets of SPR operations that can transform `T_{i_m}` to `T_{i_{m+1}}` tell us how the trees can be combined" (2003, Section 3.7), with worked examples (2005, Figures 7, 9). The constructions here are that, made precise, in both directions.

Gusfield et al. 2007 use it at line 656, to prove `R¹(M_d) <= 3d` in Theorem 11.

`Bound.lean` proves `R_le_sprLength` by that construction of an ancestral recombination graph from a sequence of trees, with `L(P)` in `ℕ∞`, because `d_oSPR` is infinite between trees that no sequence of ordered-SPR operations connects. Going along the sites:

- The network starts as the first tree, with a root above it (`hasState_init`).
- A site is placed on the edge of the current tree above its cluster (`HasState.addSite`). Its state changes at the nodes below that arc, following the arcs to the right of every crossover so far, since the new site is to the right of them.
- An ordered-SPR operation on the cluster `A` is one new recombination node `x` just above the node of `A` (`HasState.spr`, `Realizes.spr`). Its parents are the old parent of the node, on the left of the crossover, and a node at the time of the new parent of `A`, on the right. Since the times of the nodes are kept, and the new parent is
  earlier than `A` (`TimeOrderedTree.time_lt`), this closes no cycle. This is where time-ordered is used.

The state of the construction is `Realizes`: every arc goes forward in time, and a node at time `t` on the path up from a row has below it exactly the rows of the edge of the current tree above that row at time `t` (`lin`). All the nodes on the path are covered, including those of earlier trees, and a time that isn't taken gets a new node (`exists_node_at`).

If the operation returns `A` to the old parent, the new node is an ordinary node and there's no recombination.

**The other inequality, so `min L(P) = R¹(M)`.** `Minimal.lean` goes from a network to trees, as the source says: "to each ARG corresponding to a set of length-`ℓ` DNA sequences, one can associate a unique length-`ℓ` sequence `P` of trees". A *sampling* keeps one arc into each recombination node, and its tree has the rows below each node as clusters, with a rank along the arcs as times (`sampledTree`). The tree of a site follows the crossovers at that site, and it's compatible with the column (`keptReach_iff_label_ne`, `exists_choices`). Changing the kept arc at one node is one ordered-SPR operation, or no change at all (`same_or_isOrderedSPR`), which is the source's `d_SPR = d_rec` in the direction that was missing. So a network with `R` recombination nodes gives `L(P) ≤ R` (`exists_sprLength_le`), and `R¹(M)` is the minimum (`exists_sprLength_eq_R`, `R_eq_iInf_sprLength`).

`BinaryPaths.lean` has this for the source's own class: binary trees with distinct times, and the distance through such trees (`IsOrdered`, `dOrdered`, `orderedLength`, `exists_orderedLength_eq_R`). A network can have at most two arcs out of each node, by splitting nodes (`exists_outDegree_le_two`), and then its sampled trees are in that class (`isOrdered_sampledTree`).

The hypothesis `NoConstantColumn` is needed: a constant column has no compatible tree in Lean, by the definition of line 646 of Gusfield et al. The source calls every tree compatible with it.

Not formalized, from these papers: the running of the algorithm of (4), (5), that is, computing `min L(P)` by dynamic programming, the modified algorithm of its Section 3.6, the data reduction of its Section 3.7, and its Proposition 4 of 2003. Nothing else uses them.

Imports: `Gusfield2007.TimeOrdered` for the definitions, `Gusfield2007.NetworkOps` for `PreNet` and for trimming.
